name: hashify
workload: Median per-lookup time (criterion) on real key sets (HTTP methods, IMAP commands, Sieve keywords, charset names, HTML entities) and synthetic 10k/100k random string keys, for sequential 'hits' and pseudo-random 'random' lookup patterns
claimed_speedup: hashify's map! macro is 4.1x-12.6x faster than the phf crate's default CHD layout and 3.2x-8.8x faster than phf's experimental ptrhash layout across all tested key sets; also faster than a plain Rust match for larger key sets (e.g. 25.1-39.8ns for match vs 1.85-1.95ns for hashify on the 2125-entry HTML-entity table)
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.98, criterion default release settings (opt-level=3 noted separately for the build-time table)
tradeoffs: Rust-only procedural macro; tables are built at proc-macro expansion time so a large key set adds real build time (up to ~24s for 1,000,000 keys, worse without opt-level=3); cannot rebuild tables at runtime; not usable from C++
caveats: Benchmark is first-party (project's own README/criterion suite), but hardware, Rust version, and exact bench commands are all stated and reproducible (cargo bench --bench lookup), satisfying Tier A; no independent third-party confirmation found this session

name: mph (qlibs)
workload: Lookup of small compile-time-known string/int static maps (5-149 entries: random strings of length 4, 8, mixed 1-8, and random uint keys) run with the qlibs/mph benchmark harness against std::map, std::unordered_map, boost::unordered_map, boost::flat_map, and gperf-generated C code
claimed_speedup: mph is fastest in every row under both g++ and clang++: e.g. random_strings_5_len_4 - std::unordered_map 5.56ns vs mph 1.61ns (~3.5x); random_strings_100_len_8 - std::unordered_map 15.32ns vs mph 1.58ns (~9.7x), gperf 8.04ns vs mph 1.58ns (~5.1x)
tradeoffs: Requires C++20 (gcc-12+/clang-15+); keys/values must be fully known at compile time (constexpr array), not a general dynamic hash table; author states it targets thousands, not millions, of entries; optional bmi2/SIMD hardware acceleration
caveats: First-party benchmark; compiler and flags are stated but no CPU model is given, so this is capped at Tier C per the rules (partial methodology) even though the numbers themselves look plausible (3-10x, not an outlier ratio) and are not independently reproduced
found_via: gh search repos "perfect hash" --sort stars; gh api repos/qlibs/mph/readme

name: fph-table (Flash Perfect Hash)
workload: Lookup (successful 'find') of 64-bit integer keys at 0.9 max_load_factor across table sizes from 32 to 10^7, run by the independent hashtable-bench suite across std::unordered_map, ska::flat_hash_map, absl::flat_hash_map, tsl::robin_map, emhash7, robin_hood, and fph::DynamicFphMap/MetaFphMap
claimed_speedup: fph::DynamicFphMap (with fph::SimpleSeedHash) has the fastest lookup once the table exceeds ~1,000 elements on x86-64 (AMD 3990X) and the fastest lookup at every tested size on arm64 (Apple M1 Max), ahead of std::unordered_map and every other tested map in the hashtable-bench charts; a second independent suite (Martin Ankerl's 2022 hashmap benchmark, Intel i7-8700 @3200MHz, clang++13 -O3 -march=native) separately reports fph::DynamicFphMap find as 'extremely fast, regardless of the hash'
compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.2.0 -O3 (AMD 3990X, Ubuntu 20.04, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release); clang 13.1.6 (Apple M1 Max, macOS 12.1); separately clang++13 -O3 -march=native on the Ankerl benchmark
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3990X (Zen2); Apple M1 Max; Intel Xeon E-2388G (Rocket Lake, per the hashtable-bench blog); Intel i7-8700 @3200MHz (Ankerl benchmark)
tradeoffs: Dynamic perfect hash table rebuilds the whole table whenever an insert breaks perfectness, so insert/erase are slow and are 'the slowest in the benchmark' per the Ankerl suite; needs a seed-aware hash functor (not plain std::hash) unless using the no-seed branch; keys must be CopyConstructible, values MoveConstructible; MetaFphMap trades hit-lookup speed for faster miss-lookup
caveats: Exact ns/op figures live in PNG charts in hashtable-bench and in a normalized (base-100) interactive table on Ankerl's blog, not as machine-readable numbers pulled into this record; hashtable-bench is maintained by the same author as fph-table (though it independently tests many third-party maps), while the Ankerl suite is fully independent
found_via: gh search repos "perfect hash" --sort stars; WebSearch "perfect hash C++ library faster than unordered_map github 2025 2026"

name: Perfect::Hash / pperf
workload: Lookup time over a 99,171-key dictionary (linux/amd64) and a medium 2,000-key dictionary, comparing generated perfect-hash C code (hanovpp/hanov/urban/pearson/cmph-* variants) and a generated switch table against gperf-generated C code
claimed_speedup: On the 99,171-key dictionary gperf fails to complete ('-1 errors... killed') while hanovpp/hanov/urban finish and achieve 0.007-0.014s total lookup time; on the 2,000-key dictionary gperf itself has the fastest lookup (0.001428s) but the slowest compile time (0.87s vs 0.08-0.14s for the Perl::Hash algorithms)
tradeoffs: The Perl module is a CPAN generator; it produces plain C output that is directly usable from C/C++. Result is nuanced: gperf actually wins on raw lookup latency for small dictionaries and only fails to scale (times out/dies) on very large ones; a plain generated switch table has an impractical 36+ second compile time and a huge generated source file. Repo is self-described as 'alpha'
caveats: Own benchmark script (examples/bench.pl); CPU model is stated but the compiler/flags used to build the generated C benchmark harness are not shown in the README, so this is capped at Tier C; treat the 'beats gperf' framing narrowly as a scalability win, not a universal speed win

name: phashtable (gsauthof)
workload: Repeated random-slot lookup micro-benchmark (probing all slots of a table built from real-world ISIN identifier strings, 2,776 to 1.4M items) comparing a 2-level perfect hash table against std::unordered_map, each combined with 3 hash functions (sdbm, SipHash, and a stock/library default), with min/max per-lookup latency measured on an isolated, frequency-locked core
claimed_speedup: On an Intel Atom C3758: ptable_sdbm latency is 43-44ns (1ns min-max spread) vs umap_sdbm 22-61ns (39ns spread); on an Intel Xeon Gold 6246: ptable_sdbm 11-12ns vs umap_sdbm 9-34ns (25ns spread). The perfect hash table is not faster in minimum-case latency (umap_sdbm's minimum is actually lower on both CPUs), but its worst-case latency and jitter are far more consistent than std::unordered_map's, whose access time varies up to ~3x due to collision resolution
compiler_and_flags: g++ -std=gnu++17 -Wall -O3 -march=goldmont-plus (Atom C3758 build); GCC 9 (Xeon Gold 6246, RHEL 7)
hardware: Intel Atom C3758 (Fedora 31, process pinned to an isolated core, frequency management disabled); Intel Xeon Gold 6246 (RHEL 7, isolated core, frequency locked to 4.1GHz)
tradeoffs: Static/rebuild-only table (no incremental insert/delete, meant to be built at startup or re-init); ~8.6 bytes/item overhead vs ~5.33 bytes/item for a 75%-loaded open-addressing hash table; gperf comparison in its own docs notes gperf doesn't terminate in reasonable time on the same 1.4M-key ISIN set
caveats: The project's actual claim is about latency *jitter*/worst-case consistency, not raw average speed: std::unordered_map's best-case latency is lower than the perfect hash table's on both tested CPUs, so 'faster' only clearly holds for tail latency and consistency, not the mean/min case; benchmark hardware and compiler flags for the C++ side are fully stated (build-bench.sh), so despite the nuance this is graded Tier A on methodology
found_via: WebSearch "perfect hash C++ library faster than unordered_map github 2025 2026"

name: static_maps
workload: Construction + lookup runtime on three demos run 10,000+ times each: (1) average isotopic mass lookup by element symbol (1024 random lookups per run), (2) amino-acid-from-codon translation (65,536 codons per run), (3) in-place random modification of S&P 500 stock prices by ticker symbol
claimed_speedup: static_maps::unordered_map runtime is <40% of std::unordered_map on the elements demo (35.8 vs 89.6 microsec avg), <35% on the codon demo (607.6 vs 1746.8 microsec avg), and <73% on the stocks demo (~15295 vs ~21228 microsec avg); also <80%/<45%/<97% of frozen::unordered_map on the same three demos, <35% of a PTHash-based lookup, and <89% of a gperf-generated map (single demo tested for PTHash/gperf)
compiler_and_flags: g++ 15.2.1, -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native (plus -fconstexpr-ops-limit=100000000 to 20000000000 to allow compile-time construction of the larger tables; also verified to compile under clang 21.1.6 with -fconstexpr-steps raised)
hardware: Intel Core i5-1240P @4.4GHz laptop CPU, 12 cores/24 threads, 448KiB/640KiB L1, 9MiB L2, 12MiB L3 cache; nice -20, chrt -f 98 real-time priority, ASLR disabled
tradeoffs: consteval/constexpr-only: the full keyset must be known at compile time; compile time is much higher than std (e.g. 55.2s vs 1.5s for the stock demo) and requires raising the compiler's constexpr step/ops limits, sometimes to values that risk long or failing builds on large keysets; drop-in only for std::unordered_map's operator[]/at() access pattern, not the full container API (e.g. custom KeyEqual/Allocator need modification)
caveats: Code is distributed as a Figshare software deposit (DOI), not a live GitHub repo, so there is no commit history or star count to check ongoing maintenance; the figshare landing page returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch this session, so availability was confirmed only via the DOI redirect and the paper's own citation of the deposit, not by directly viewing the hosted files
found_via: arXiv export API query search_query=abs:"perfect hash" AND abs:"unordered_map" (paper arXiv:2602.22506, Myhal & Serang, Hillsdale College)

name: frozen (serge-sans-paille/frozen) -- new benchmark evidence
workload: Same three demos as the static_maps paper (element-mass, codon, and stock-symbol lookup), run independently by the static_maps authors against both frozen::unordered_map and std::unordered_map on identical hardware/compiler/build
claimed_speedup: (derived from page data) frozen::unordered_map's average runtime is roughly 50% of std::unordered_map on the elements demo (44.9 vs 89.6 microsec avg), roughly 78% on the codon demo (1365.5 vs 1746.8 microsec avg), and roughly 74% on the stocks demo (15804.5 vs 21228.1 microsec avg), computed by comparing the paper's separate frozen-vs-static_maps and std-vs-static_maps panels for the same demo
tradeoffs: Already catalogued elsewhere (frozen is on the KNOWN_LIST); this record exists solely to capture fresh, independent Tier A benchmark evidence for it found via arXiv this session
caveats: The std-vs-frozen ratio is derived by combining two separate comparison panels from the same figure/paper (each directly measured against static_maps on the same demo/hardware/compiler) rather than a single head-to-head frozen-vs-std run; frozen also has a notably higher compile time on the stock demo (21.1s vs 1.5s for std::unordered_map) due to constexpr overhead
found_via: arXiv export API query search_query=abs:"perfect hash" AND abs:"unordered_map" (paper arXiv:2602.22506)
